questions.knowledge_point: Finding an Integral Expression For the Arc Length of a Curve
questions.problem: Which integral expression gives the arc length of the curve $f(t)=⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡t+\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,{e}^{t},\,\operatorname{sin}⁡t-\operatorname{cos}⁡t⟩$ from $t=-1$ to $t=1?$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we find ${f}^{′}(t)$ and $‖{f}^{′}(t)‖:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t+\operatorname{sin}⁡t),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({e}^{t}),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡t-\operatorname{cos}⁡t)⟩ \\  & =⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡t-\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,{e}^{t},\,\operatorname{cos}⁡t+\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩ \\ ‖{f}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{(\operatorname{cos}⁡t-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)}^{2}+({e}^{t})^{2}+{(\operatorname{cos}⁡t+\operatorname{sin}⁡t)}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{cos}^{2}⁡t-2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\operatorname{sin}⁡t+{sin}^{2}⁡t+{e}^{2t}+{cos}^{2}⁡t+2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\operatorname{sin}⁡t+{sin}^{2}⁡t} \\  & =\sqrt{{e}^{2t}+2({cos}^{2}⁡t+{sin}^{2}⁡t)} \\  & =\sqrt{{e}^{2t}+2}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the arc length of the curve is

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}‖{f}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}\sqrt{{e}^{2t}+2}\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Which integral expression gives the arc length of the curve $g(t)=⟨\operatorname{sin}⁡2t,\,\operatorname{cos}⁡3t⟩$ from $t=0$ to $t=\pi ?$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we find ${g}^{′}(t)$ and $‖{g}^{′}(t)‖:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{g}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡2t),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡3t)⟩ \\  & =⟨2\operatorname{cos}⁡2t,\,-3\operatorname{sin}⁡3t⟩ \\ ‖{g}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{(2\operatorname{cos}⁡2t)^{2}+(-3\operatorname{sin}⁡3t)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{4{cos}^{2}⁡2t+9{sin}^{2}⁡3t}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the arc length of the curve is

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }‖{g}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }\sqrt{4{cos}^{2}⁡2t+9{sin}^{2}⁡3t}\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Which integral expression gives the arc length of the curve $f(t)=⟨4\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,3\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,4\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩$ from $t=\frac{\pi }{6}$ to $t=\frac{\pi }{4}?$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we find ${f}^{′}(t)$ and $‖{f}^{′}(t)‖:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(4\operatorname{cos}⁡t),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3\operatorname{sin}⁡t),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(4\operatorname{sin}⁡t)⟩ \\  & =⟨-4\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,3\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,4\operatorname{cos}⁡t⟩ \\ ‖{f}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{(-4\operatorname{sin}⁡t)^{2}+(3\operatorname{cos}⁡t)^{2}+(4\operatorname{cos}⁡t)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{16{sin}^{2}⁡t+9{cos}^{2}⁡t+16{cos}^{2}⁡t} \\  & =\sqrt{16({sin}^{2}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t)+9{cos}^{2}⁡t} \\  & =\sqrt{9{cos}^{2}⁡t+16}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the arc length of the curve is

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={\int }_{\pi /6}^{\pi /4}‖{f}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /6}^{\pi /4}\sqrt{9{cos}^{2}⁡t+16}\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Which integral  expression gives the arc length of the curve $g(t)=⟨t\operatorname{sin}⁡t,2-t\operatorname{cos}⁡t⟩$
from  $t=0$ to $t=\pi ?$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we find ${g}^{′}(t)$ and $‖{g}^{′}(t)‖:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{g}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t\operatorname{sin}⁡t),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2-t\operatorname{cos}⁡t)⟩ \\  & =⟨\operatorname{sin}⁡t+t\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,t\operatorname{sin}⁡t-\operatorname{cos}⁡t⟩ \\ ‖{g}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{(\operatorname{sin}⁡t+t\operatorname{cos}⁡t)^{2}+(t\operatorname{sin}⁡t-\operatorname{cos}⁡t)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{sin}^{2}⁡t+2t\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t+{t}^{2}{cos}^{2}⁡t+{t}^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡t-2t\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t} \\  & =\sqrt{1+{t}^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the arc length of the curve is:

$$
\begin{aligned}L={\int }_{0}^{\pi }‖{g}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t={\int }_{0}^{\pi }\sqrt{1+{t}^{2}}\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Computing the Arc Length of a Planar Curve
questions.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14052793/assets/e6de928031610e2aaf55e3dd753449f766e7dc028a6618087e7489224a73ea7d.png)

Find the arc length of the curve $r(t)=⟨t\operatorname{sin}⁡t+\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,t\operatorname{cos}⁡t-\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩$
from  $t=0$ to $t=2.$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we find ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $‖{r}^{′}(t)‖:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t\operatorname{sin}⁡t+\operatorname{cos}⁡t),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t\operatorname{cos}⁡t-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,⟩ \\  & =⟨t\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,-t\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩ \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{(t\operatorname{cos}⁡t)}^{2}+{(-t\operatorname{sin}⁡t)}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{t}^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡t+{t}^{2}{cos}^{2}⁡t} \\  & =\sqrt{{t}^{2}} \\  & =t\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that $t\ge 0$ for $t\in [0,2].$

Therefore, the arc length of the curve is

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={\int }_{0}^{2}‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}t\,\text{d}t \\  & ={(\frac{{t}^{2}}{2})|}_{0}^{2} \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Computing the Arc Length of a Planar Curve
questions.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14052793/assets/162c0d0310cbbb533c30af373820751fc6c5a447127958486571224d7f8ac07a.png)

Find the arc length of the curve $r(t)=⟨{e}^{t}\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,{e}^{t}\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩$ from $t=0$ to $t=\frac{\pi }{2}.$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we find ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $‖{r}^{′}(t)‖:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({e}^{t}\operatorname{cos}⁡t),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({e}^{t}\operatorname{sin}⁡t)⟩ \\  & =⟨{e}^{t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t-\operatorname{sin}⁡t),\,{e}^{t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t+\operatorname{sin}⁡t)⟩ \\  & ={e}^{t}⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡t-\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,\operatorname{cos}⁡t+\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩ \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =|{e}^{t}|\sqrt{{(\operatorname{cos}⁡t-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)}^{2}+{(\operatorname{cos}⁡t+\operatorname{sin}⁡t)}^{2}} \\  & ={e}^{t}\sqrt{{cos}^{2}⁡t-2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\operatorname{sin}⁡t+{sin}^{2}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t+2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\operatorname{sin}⁡t+{sin}^{2}⁡t} \\  & ={e}^{t}\sqrt{2({cos}^{2}⁡t+{sin}^{2}⁡t)} \\  & =\sqrt{2}{e}^{t}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the arc length of the curve is

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\sqrt{2}{e}^{t}\,\text{d}t \\  & =\sqrt{2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{e}^{t}\,\text{d}t \\  & =\sqrt{2}{e}^{t}\,{|}_{0}^{\pi /2} \\  & =\sqrt{2}({e}^{\pi /2}-{e}^{0}) \\  & =\sqrt{2}({e}^{\pi /2}-1).\end{aligned}
$$

Find the arc length of the curve $r(t)=⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡2t+2t\operatorname{sin}⁡2t,\,\operatorname{sin}⁡2t-2t\operatorname{cos}⁡2t⟩$
from  $t=1$ to $t=2.$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we find ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $‖{r}^{′}(t)‖:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡2t+2t\operatorname{sin}⁡2t),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡2t-2t\operatorname{cos}⁡2t)⟩ \\  & =⟨4t\operatorname{cos}⁡2t\,,4t\operatorname{sin}⁡2t⟩ \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{(4t\operatorname{cos}⁡2t)}^{2}+{(4t\operatorname{sin}⁡2t)}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{16{t}^{2}{cos}^{2}⁡t+16{t}^{2}{sin}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{16{t}^{2}} \\  & =4t\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that $t>0$ for $t\in [1,2].$

Therefore, the arc length of the curve is

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={\int }_{1}^{2}‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}4t\,\text{d}t \\  & =2{t}^{2}{|}_{1}^{2} \\  & =2(4-1) \\  & =6.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14052793/assets/54cd1a0532bbdbe76bd81d5ad737f6d3e9f5293d08ea78758865b3b71850e346.png)

Find the arc length of the curve $g(t)=⟨\operatorname{ln}⁡t-\frac{{t}^{2}}{2},\,2t⟩$ from $t=1$ to $t=e.$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we find ${g}^{′}(t)$ and $‖{g}^{′}(t)‖:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{g}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{ln}⁡t-\frac{{t}^{2}}{2}),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2t)⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{1}{t}-t,\,2⟩ \\ ‖{g}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{(\frac{1}{t}-t)}^{2}+{2}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{1}{{t}^{2}}-2+{t}^{2}+4} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{1}{{t}^{2}}+2+{t}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{(\frac{1}{t}+t)}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{1}{t}+t\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the arc length of the curve is

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={\int }_{1}^{e}‖{g}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{e}(\frac{1}{t}+t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =(\operatorname{ln}⁡t+\frac{{t}^{2}}{2}){|}_{1}^{e} \\  & =(\operatorname{ln}⁡e+\frac{{e}^{2}}{2})-(\operatorname{ln}⁡1+\frac{{1}^{2}}{2}) \\  & =1+\frac{{e}^{2}}{2}-0-\frac{1}{2} \\  & =\frac{{e}^{2}+1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Computing the Arc Length of a Three-Dimensional Spatial Curve
questions.problem:
Find the arc length of the curve $r(t)=⟨2t\operatorname{cos}⁡2t-\operatorname{sin}⁡2t,\,\frac{3{t}^{2}}{2},\,2t\operatorname{sin}⁡2t+\operatorname{cos}⁡2t⟩$
from  $t=0$ to $t=2.$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we find ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $‖{r}^{′}(t)‖:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2t\operatorname{cos}⁡2t-\operatorname{sin}⁡2t),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{3{t}^{2}}{2}),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2t\operatorname{sin}⁡2t+\operatorname{cos}⁡2t)⟩ \\  & =⟨-4t\operatorname{sin}⁡2t,\,3t,\,4t\operatorname{cos}⁡2t⟩ \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{(-4t\operatorname{sin}⁡2t)}^{2}+(3t)^{2}+{(4t\operatorname{cos}⁡2t)}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{16{t}^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡2t+9{t}^{2}+16{t}^{2}{cos}^{2}⁡2t} \\  & =\sqrt{16{t}^{2}+9{t}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{25{t}^{2}} \\  & =5t\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that $t\ge 0$ for $t\in [0,2].$

Therefore, the arc length of the curve is

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={\int }_{0}^{2}‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}5t\,\text{d}t \\  & ={(\frac{5{t}^{2}}{2})|}_{0}^{2} \\  & =10.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Find the arc length of the curve $r(t)=⟨{t}^{2},\,4,\,{t}^{2}⟩$
from  $t=0$ to $t=2.$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we find ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $‖{r}^{′}(t)‖:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2}),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(4),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2})⟩ \\  & =⟨2t,\,0,\,2t⟩ \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{(2t)}^{2}+0+{(2t)}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{8{t}^{2}} \\  & =2\sqrt{2}\,t\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that $t\ge 0$ for $t\in [0,2].$

Therefore, the arc length of the curve is

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={\int }_{0}^{2}‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}2\sqrt{2}t\,\text{d}t \\  & =\sqrt{2}({t}^{2}){|}_{0}^{2} \\  & =4\sqrt{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Find the arc length of the curve $f(t)=⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡t+t\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,\operatorname{sin}⁡t-t\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}{t}^{2}⟩$
from $t=1$ to $t=3.$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we find ${f}^{′}(t)$ and $‖{f}^{′}(t)‖:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t+t\operatorname{sin}⁡t),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡t-t\operatorname{cos}⁡t),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}{t}^{2})⟩ \\  & =⟨-\operatorname{sin}⁡t+(\operatorname{sin}⁡t+t\operatorname{cos}⁡t),\,\operatorname{cos}⁡t-(\operatorname{cos}⁡t-t\operatorname{sin}⁡t),\,\sqrt{3}t⟩ \\  & =⟨t\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,t\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,\sqrt{3}t⟩ \\ ‖{f}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{(t\operatorname{cos}⁡t)^{2}+(t\operatorname{sin}⁡t)^{2}+(\sqrt{3}t)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{t}^{2}({cos}^{2}⁡t+{sin}^{2}⁡t)+3{t}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{4{t}^{2}} \\  & =2t\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that $t>0$ for $t\in [1,3].$

Therefore, the arc length of the curve is

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={\int }_{1}^{3}‖{f}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{3}2t\,\text{d}t \\  & ={t}^{2}{|}_{1}^{3} \\  & =9-1 \\  & =8.\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.problem:
Write down the integral that gives the arc length of the curve  $\mathbf f (t) = \langle 3 \sin t, \: 2\sin 2t \rangle$
from $t =\dfrac {3\pi} 2$  to $t = 2\pi.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14052793/assets/574a16e843a9c81e5fc9ddbbe2c0dc2c308ffcac4991bcbf48c7f45b4871c93b.png)
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
First, we find $\mathbf f'(t)$ and $\|\mathbf f'(t)\|\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3\operatorname{sin}⁡t),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2\operatorname{sin}⁡2t)⟩ \\  & =⟨3\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,4\operatorname{cos}⁡2t⟩ \\ ‖{f}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{(3\operatorname{cos}⁡t)^{2}+(4\operatorname{cos}⁡2t)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{9{cos}^{2}⁡t+16{cos}^{2}⁡2t}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the arc length of the curve is

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={\int }_{a}^{b}‖{f}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{3\pi /2}^{2\pi }\sqrt{9{cos}^{2}⁡t+16{cos}^{2}⁡2t}\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.problem:
Find the arc length of the curve $\mathbf g (t) = \langle 3 - 2 \sin 2t, \: 1 - 2\cos 2t \rangle$ from $t=\dfrac \pi 3$ to $\pi.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14052793/assets/29c97e5963d451cc389944ef113764b2d15998448e773a02bb98c062207c2860.png)
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
First, we find $\mathbf g'(t)$ and $\|\mathbf g'(t)\|\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{g}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3-2\operatorname{sin}⁡2t),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(1-2\operatorname{cos}⁡2t)⟩ \\  & =⟨-4\operatorname{cos}⁡2t,\,4\operatorname{sin}⁡2t⟩ \\ ‖{g}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{(-4\operatorname{cos}⁡2t)^{2}+(4\operatorname{sin}⁡2t)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{16{cos}^{2}⁡2t+16{sin}^{2}⁡2t} \\  & =\sqrt{16} \\  & =4\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the arc length of the curve is

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={\int }_{a}^{b}‖{g}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /3}^{\pi }4\,\text{d}t \\  & =4t\,{|}_{\pi /3}^{\pi } \\  & =4(\pi -\frac{\pi }{3}) \\  & =\frac{8\pi }{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14052793/assets/8573aedcd26cba038b2db072560cd3d6ba7676542888a2d9b8a356713eaf6724.png)

Find the arc length of the curve $\mathbf r (t) = \langle \sin t ,\: \cos t, \: t \rangle$
from  $t =0$ to $t = 2\pi.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
First, we find $\mathbf r'(t)$ and $\|\mathbf r'(t)\|\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡t),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)⟩ \\  & =⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,-\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,1⟩ \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{(\operatorname{cos}⁡t)^{2}+(-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)^{2}+{1}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{cos}^{2}⁡t+{sin}^{2}⁡t+1} \\  & =\sqrt{1+1} \\  & =\sqrt{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the arc length of the curve is

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\sqrt{2}\,\text{d}t \\  & =\text{ }\sqrt{2}\,t{|}_{0}^{2\pi } \\  & =\sqrt{2}(2\pi -0) \\  & =2\sqrt{2}\pi .\end{aligned}
$$
